synthesis.headline: Plains severe storms and flash flooding ahead of western closed low; Simon stalls off Mexico
synthesis.narrative:
The main story today is a slow-moving front from the Texas Big Bend to the Corn Belt, fed by Gulf moisture as a closed low pushes toward the Four Corners. SPC has a Slight risk over Kansas, northwest Missouri and the southern High Plains. Storms should fire along the front and dryline around 21Z in low-90s heat and mid-to-upper-60s dewpoints. Early supercells could bring 65-75 mph gusts, large hail and a tornado or two, then grow into clusters over Kansas, Missouri and Illinois overnight. WPC has a Slight flood risk from the Hill Country to western Missouri, with 2-4 inches possible through Thursday. Hurricane Simon, down from yesterday's Category 3 to 80 kt and 977 mb, is crawling west-northwest at 3 mph about 95 miles west of Cabo Corrientes. A Hurricane Warning covers Las Islas Marias, and coastal west-central Mexico faces 5-10 inches of rain, locally near 15 in Sinaloa, by Thursday. EP93 to the southeast is expected to become a depression or storm today. A new New England low brings soaking rain and mountain snow, the West sees first freezes, and the Midwest and Southeast could set record highs.

At 500 mb, a cold closed low sits over the West with its trough reaching Baja. WPC and SPC place it near the Four Corners, matching the dry core over Nevada-Utah on satellite; the 12Z chart summary puts it farther west. Downstream, a broad ridge covers the Rockies and Plains, with 590-592 dam heights along the Gulf. Southwest flow between them lifts Gulf air over the front. A smaller cold low over the Great Lakes is moving off to the Northeast. Simon sits in weak steering currents, and its slow motion means upwelling and drawn-out rain. NHC expects little net motion for 60 hours, shear and dry air cutting it to 55 kt by day 4, and a northward turn on days 4-5, with very low track confidence.

On Wednesday the front moves into the Ozarks, Ohio Valley and Mid-Atlantic. SPC has a Marginal risk, mainly for wind, from southwest Texas to the Ozarks and from the upper Ohio Valley to the Mid-Atlantic. The Slight flood risk shifts to a Texas-Arkansas-western Kentucky line. On Friday and Saturday a deep trough drives a strong low from the Great Lakes into Atlantic Canada, with high winds, lake-effect rain and snow, and widespread frost and freeze into early next week. Leftover western-low energy plus Simon's moisture keep locally heavy rain over the southern High Plains through Friday. The cold snap is temporary, not a pattern change. CPC's 6-10 day heights rebuild a +12 dam center over the Great Lakes, and the 8-14 day map keeps +9 dam over the Upper Midwest, with a strong ridge near Greenland at both leads. WPC brings warmth back to the north-central US this weekend, ahead of a new western trough Monday.
synthesis.climate_context: A strong El Niño frames the season. The Oceanic Niño Index reached +2.16 C for July-September, up from -0.39 last winter and rising about 0.36 C per season through the latest reading. That fits an eastern Pacific hurricane season still producing in mid-October: Simon, with EP93 close behind. Meanwhile the Atlantic is quiet, its one disturbance stuck under strong upper winds with near-zero chances. Over land, mid-October is the fall secondary severe season. The Plains threat depends on deep Gulf moisture under an unusually warm ridge, the same airmass behind possible record highs. CPC's teleconnection indices are 13 days stale and not used here.
synthesis.regional_notes: No SPC mesoscale discussions active. SPC also flags isolated severe storms in parts of New York today, with a brief tornado possible. Simon is very small: hurricane-force winds reach only about 10 miles from the center. Las Islas Marias faces dangerous storm surge, and a Hurricane Watch north of Escuinapa to Bahia Tempehuaya could see hurricane conditions Thursday. Most hail risk Wednesday is in southwest Texas. Canada: a deep 967-968 mb low in the Greenland/North Atlantic sector, and brisk winds along a front over Quebec and Labrador.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This 0900Z analysis shows a broad, fairly weak pattern across the CONUS, with no deep surface low. The strongest closed features are a cluster of lows from the northern Plains into the upper Midwest: a low near 1009 mb over the eastern Dakotas/northwest Minnesota, a 1006 mb low over eastern Montana/western Dakotas with a smaller 1006-1007 mb center nearby, and lows of about 1001 mb and 1006 mb near the Great Lakes. Highs are modest, mostly 1017-1022 mb: roughly 1017 mb over the north-central Plains and central Canada, 1021-1022 mb near the Pacific Northwest coast, a 1019 mb high off the Southeast coast, and a 1029 mb high near the Mid-Atlantic. None of these is strong enough to be worth much explanatory weight on its own. A 1013 mb center over Mexico is a weak feature, and Hurricane Simon is boxed at lower left with max winds of 80 kt gusting to 100 kt.

Fronts include a long cold front extending from the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies down through the Great Basin and southern California into the eastern Pacific, with a second cold front crossing the northern Great Lakes and Ontario. A warm or stationary boundary stretches from the central Plains east-northeast through Missouri toward the Ohio Valley, near the 400-500 km latitude band of the analysis. Another cold front sweeps through the Northeast and New England, with a trailing boundary down the Atlantic coast.

The pressure gradient looks tightest over the northern Rockies and northern Plains, where several lows crowd close to the 1017-1022 mb highs, and along the Pacific Northwest coast. Gradients are slack across the southern Plains, Gulf Coast, and Southeast, where isobars are widely spaced.

The surface pattern focuses lift along the Plains-to-Ohio Valley warm/stationary boundary and the northern-tier cold fronts, with warm, moist air (dewpoints in the 60s and low 70s) streaming north across the southern Plains and Mississippi Valley. Convergence near the Great Lakes lows and the Northeast cold front is the other obvious lift axis.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This CMC surface analysis, valid 00Z Tuesday 13 October 2026, is drawn on a polar projection, so the upper half of the frame is Arctic Ocean, the Archipelago and Greenland sector rather than southern Canada. Several lows near the pole and the Archipelago (986 mb near the top centre, 986 mb just to its lower right, and a cluster of 984 to 995 mb centres across the central Archipelago and Baffin Bay side) form a broad, multi-centred low-pressure region, with a separate 968/967/973 mb complex on the right side of the frame in what appears to be the Greenland and North Atlantic sector. That is a deep system, though its position relative to coastlines is hard to pin down at this chart scale.

Over mainland Canada the pattern is more subdued. A 995 mb low sits in the northwestern interior, with a trailing front curving southward on its western flank, and a 1029 mb high anchors the area to its west over the far northwest. Further south, a long frontal boundary arcs from the Great Lakes and Hudson Bay region northeastward toward Labrador and Quebec, where the most closely packed isobars appear, indicating a tight gradient and likely brisk winds along the front. A 1024 mb high sits to the south of this boundary, and the implied flow around it would support southerly return flow toward the cold front on the east side.

The cross-border link is clearest in the east. A 1001 mb low on the Ontario-Quebec side of the US border region is tied to a front running southwest across the Great Lakes toward the central US, with a second boundary and 992 and 1000 mb lows near the Atlantic coast, consistent with a progressive frontal system moving offshore. Across the western and central United States the pressure field is flat, with highs of 1017 to 1025 mb and weak lows near 1005 mb in the southwest, so the sharpest contrasts in this analysis are concentrated north of the border and in the Arctic rather than over the continental US.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary:
The 1200 UTC 13 Oct 2026 500 mb analysis shows a deep closed low off the Pacific Northwest and northern California coast, with the heaviest shading (wind speeds of roughly 70-80 kt in the dark red core) wrapped around the low center near 130W. Labeled contours there reach about 5,600 m (560 dam), and the cyclonic circulation looks closed with a cold pool (around -20 C or colder) beneath it, so this appears to be a genuinely cut-off, self-retaining system rather than an open wave. Its associated trough axis extends southward along the California coast into northern Baja, where a green wind band wraps down the Pacific side, implying a deep, nearly neutral to slightly negative-tilted trough.

Downstream, heights rise sharply across the interior West: a broad ridge covers the Rockies and Plains, with contours near 5,800-5,900 m (580-590 dam) over the southern Plains and 590-592 dam along the Gulf Coast under the subtropical ridge, marked by the H over the western Gulf. A smaller closed circulation with its own cold core sits near the Great Lakes and Ontario (values around -10 to -14 C, heights near 5,600-5,800 m), producing a secondary maximum in wind speed (about 50-60 kt, brownish shading) from the Great Lakes into New England. This is an eastern shortwave or weak closed low with a progressive character, exiting toward the Northeast.

Overall the pattern is amplified and not zonal, but it should not be called a Rex block: there is no anticyclone plainly poleward of the western cutoff low. What is plotted is a deep Pacific coast cutoff low with a ridge downstream over the central US and a separate, mobile low in the Great Lakes, a wave-train look with the western system likely quasi-stationary while the eastern one moves out. Jet-level winds are strongest on the southern and eastern flank of the western low and across the northern tier from the Great Lakes to the Northeast, so the implied jet corridor follows the periphery of both lows, with weaker flow over the central ridge and Gulf.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
The most striking feature is a compact orange-red dry area over the Great Basin, centered near the Nevada–Utah border, with an elongated dry band extending northeast across Idaho, Montana and the northern Plains toward the Canadian border. Its sharpest, most saturated core sits at the southwest end, and a dark-blue and purple cold dry airmass hugs the Pacific coast and offshore, consistent with an upper trough sitting just west of the coast. The dry band lies on the cyclonic side of the implied flow, so it is plausibly a stratospheric-intrusion-type feature, though the image alone does not establish descent.

A broad mix of dry orange and brown tones extends across the central and northern Plains into the Midwest and Ohio Valley, with scattered mid-level cloud patches in Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. East of the Rockies the imagery trends toward olive and green, and a large dark-green moist tongue covers the Gulf of Mexico and Florida.

The sharpest airmass boundary runs from near the Carolina coast southwest across the western Atlantic, with a ribbon of orange and brown dry air north of dark green moist air. That contrast marks the likely jet corridor offshore and implies strong baroclinicity along the East Coast and western Atlantic.

Organized cloud is limited. A cloud shield with embedded bright spots lies over southern Ontario, Quebec and northern New England, associated with a system near the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence region. In the south, deep convection is clearest as a bright, compact cluster over the eastern Pacific off southwestern Mexico, with a second cluster over the southern Bay of Campeche and scattered convection across the Caribbean and Hispaniola.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
This 13 Oct 2026 13:20Z Air Mass RGB shows a clear contrast between the tropics and the middle and high latitudes. Over the North Atlantic, a sharp green-to-orange airmass boundary arcs from the Gulf Coast and Florida northeastward toward a large, comma-shaped white cloud shield near the upper-right limb, suggesting a mature extratropical cyclone with its frontal band trailing southwest. That boundary approximates the polar jet corridor, though the chart shows airmass contrast rather than wind. Dry orange-red air wraps around the cyclone's western flank, consistent with descending dry air behind the system, and the elongated reddish band north of it near the limb reads as a high-PV, stratospheric-influenced feature on the cyclonic side of the flow. Over Canada and the Arctic, the limb view is heavily foreshortened, so the broad orange-purple field shows dry upper air but few details can be placed with confidence.

Across the tropics, a second, weaker moist-to-dry boundary runs from the Greater Antilles eastward across the Atlantic near the limb, marking the northern edge of the tropical moisture plume. Organized convection appears as bright white clusters over the eastern Pacific south and southwest of Mexico, near the Gulf of Tehuantepec, and off Central America's Pacific coast. A band of mid-sized clusters lies over the Caribbean south of Cuba and across northern South America. Further clusters sit over the tropical Atlantic near the right limb, and another over the Amazon basin. Loose cirrus streaks over the equatorial Pacific suggest outflow rather than strongly organized systems.

In the Southern Hemisphere, a prominent frontal cloud band curves across the southeast Pacific off Chile, and a cutoff-like cyclonic swirl with wrapped dry air sits near the Argentine coast, east of the Andes south of the Rio de la Plata region. Convection over southern Brazil and northern Argentina lies on the equatorward side of that system, with another frontal band extending into the South Atlantic.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary:
This outlook, valid October 18-22, 2026, favors above-normal temperatures across most of the central and eastern U.S., with the strongest signal centered on the Upper Midwest. The darkest shading (70-80% chance of above normal) covers the Dakotas, Minnesota, Iowa, Wisconsin, Michigan, northern Missouri and Illinois, and eastern Nebraska. Probabilities step down smoothly to 60-70% over the Plains, Mid-South and Gulf Coast, 50-60% over Texas, the Southeast and the central Rockies, and 33-50% across the northern Rockies, the Desert Southwest, the Mid-Atlantic and the Carolina coast. Hawaii is also leaning above normal, mostly in the 40-60% range.

Below-normal odds are confined to the Pacific Northwest and northern California, where a small 40-50% core sits over northwest California and southwest Oregon inside a broader 33-40% area, and to northern New England, where Maine shows 40-50% with weaker odds across New Hampshire and Vermont. Near-normal areas (equal chances) include the Great Basin and southern California, the immediate Northeast coastal corridor, and most of Alaska.

Because this chart plots probabilities of tercile categories rather than temperature departures or a height field, any inference about the upper-level pattern is only an implied reading. The warm center over the Upper Midwest with cool edges on both coasts is consistent with a western trough and a downstream ridge, with a possible weaker trough near the Northeast. The smooth gradient of probabilities from the Rockies eastward fits a broad, coherent regime rather than a transient feature. The outlook itself shows no sign of breakdown, since the warm signal is strongest in the center of the country. Whether that pattern holds beyond day 10 cannot be read from this chart. It would need the 8-14 day outlook or the height forecasts to confirm.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly prognostic, made 12 Oct 2026 and valid Oct 18-22. Contours are labeled in meters (5100, 5460, 5700, 5880 m, i.e. roughly 510-588 dam), and the dashed anomaly lines are labeled in meters as well (30, 90, 120), so the anomaly numbers cannot be dam; they read as plain meters, which I take to be up to about 12 dam at the strongest center. Anomaly values near 150 on the far right would be a misread if taken as dam, so I treat them as meters at the Greenland/Baffin Island edge of the chart.

The dominant positive anomaly centers are over the Great Lakes and Ontario, with a closed center near 120 m just north of Lake Erie, and a strong positive center near 150 m over the Greenland sector at upper right. A weaker positive center near 90 m sits over the northeast Pacific at far left. The negative anomaly center is the deep polar vortex over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago near 75N, 100W, with a minimum near -90 m, and a weaker trough signal of about -30 m appears along the Pacific Northwest and British Columbia coast, extending south toward the Great Basin.

The contours show a ridge axis running north-northeast from the Gulf Coast and Mississippi Valley through the Great Lakes into eastern Canada, with a trough axis along the West Coast, so the pattern is not a western ridge. Positive anomalies are therefore centered east of the Rockies, not over western North America. The zero-anomaly line (purple dashed) runs near the Pacific Northwest coast and southward through the interior West, meaning the near-normal to slightly negative heights hold across the West and the positive anomalies are confined to roughly the Mississippi Valley eastward.

On amplification, the flow across the northern tier is fairly zonal and tightly packed, with 5400 to 5700 m contours stacked from the northern Rockies to the Great Lakes, while the Greenland-side ridge and Arctic vortex give high-latitude meridional structure. The implied pattern is a warm, ridged East under zonal Pacific flow, with a cooler northwest trough.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 8-14 day 500 mb heights and departures chart, made 12 Oct 2026 and valid Oct 20-26. Solid green contours are heights in meters (labels run from 5160 to 5880, i.e. roughly 516-588 dam), and dashed lines are departures at 60 m intervals (about 6 dam), with red positive and blue negative; the labels on the dashed lines (30, 60, 90) are in meters, so the strongest positive center is on the order of +9 dam, not a 90 dam anomaly.

The main positive anomaly axis runs north-south through the central part of the continent, with the highest departures (labeled 90 m) over the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes region, near and just west of Lake Superior and Lake Michigan. Positive anomalies extend northward through central Canada, with the dashed red lines reaching toward Hudson Bay and the Canadian Arctic Archipelago. The ridge is therefore centered over the north-central U.S. and south-central Canada, with the 5580 and 5640 contours bulging poleward there, rather than retreated toward the Southwest or northern Mexico. Positive departures also cover much of the Plains and northern Rockies, though the core sits east of the Rockies.

A second, strong positive center sits near Greenland and the northeast Atlantic, with closed red contours reaching about 90 m (+15 dam by the labels visible), implying a high-latitude blocking-type ridge there. Weak positive anomalies also appear over the far western Pacific and the Alaska/Yukon sector.

Negative departures appear in two places: a broad area over the Arctic and northern Canadian Archipelago (blue contours labeled -60), consistent with a deep polar vortex near 5160 m, and a weaker region over Labrador, the Maritimes and the adjacent northwest Atlantic. Zero lines (purple) run through the Pacific Northwest and southern U.S., so the West Coast and Southwest sit near normal. The implied flow is a strong poleward-bulging ridge in the center of the continent with the polar vortex displaced toward the Arctic.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 1)
sources.summary:
The Day 1 outlook, valid 12Z Tuesday Oct 13 to 12Z Wednesday Oct 14, 2026, shows only two categories: a green Marginal (at least 5%) and a yellow Slight (at least 15%). No Moderate or High area is drawn. The risk areas form a single elongated southwest-to-northeast band, running from the Rio Grande border region of south Texas, through central and north Texas, across much of Oklahoma and eastern Kansas, and into Missouri, with the Marginal edge reaching the Illinois side of the Mississippi Valley near the northeast tip.

The Slight risk, the highest category on the chart, occupies the core of that band from roughly the Texas Hill Country northeastward through central Oklahoma into eastern Kansas and western Missouri. The Marginal area wraps around it and extends farther in both directions, down toward the Texas border with Mexico and up toward the central Mississippi Valley.

The narrow, linear orientation suggests the risk is tied to a slow-moving or stalled frontal boundary, perhaps with repeated storm development along it, though the chart itself does not show a front. There is no sign of a tropical system, and the band lies mostly over the Plains and Texas lowlands rather than being anchored to terrain.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 2)
sources.summary:
This Day 2 outlook, valid 12Z Wednesday October 14 to 12Z Thursday October 15, 2026, shows only two categories: a Slight risk (yellow, at least 15%) embedded within a broader Marginal risk (green, at least 5%). No Moderate or High area is drawn. The risk zone forms a long, narrow southwest-to-northeast band, starting at the Rio Grande border region of far southern Texas and stretching across much of central and eastern Texas and Oklahoma, into Arkansas, western Tennessee and Kentucky, and then toward the southern Ohio Valley.

The Slight risk core follows the same orientation, running from the Texas–Mexico border area through central Texas and eastern Oklahoma into Arkansas, then narrowing northeastward across the Mississippi Valley into western Kentucky and the Ohio Valley region. The Marginal risk wraps this core on both sides and extends farther northeast, reaching the central Appalachians and the Ohio Valley, with the green label placed near the Kentucky and West Virginia area. The band's elongated, nearly linear shape suggests a frontal or stationary boundary orientation, though the chart itself shows only risk categories and does not depict fronts or moisture.

Without the Day 1 chart alongside, I can't say whether the risk has grown, shifted or relaxed from the earlier outlook for this system.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary:
WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion, issued 400 AM EDT Tue Oct 13 2026, valid through 12Z Thu Oct 15.

A closed low approaching the Four Corners will keep cool, wet weather west of the Rockies for 48 hours. Showers and thunderstorms shift into the Heartland as the system and a Gulf ridge pull unstable air north toward a slow-moving front. Heavy rain and scattered flash flooding are expected from the Corn Belt to the Texas Big Bend, with storm totals of 2-4 inches possible through Thursday. Widely scattered severe storms today from Kansas City to Lubbock could produce large hail, damaging winds, and a tornado or two. In New England, a developing low brings soaking rain and some elevation snow today.

Unseasonable warmth continues over the Midwest and Southeast for a few more days, with several daily record highs possible. The West has numerous first freezes this morning. By late week, reinforcing Canadian cold air will push the front southward, bringing fall-like weather to much of the Central U.S.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook, issued 0752 AM CDT Tue Oct 13 2026, valid through 12Z Oct 14. A slight risk of severe thunderstorms covers northwest Missouri, Kansas, and the southern High Plains. Widely scattered severe storms with large hail, damaging winds, and a possible tornado are expected from the central and southern Plains into the Lower Missouri Valley this afternoon and tonight. Convective initiation is expected along a sharpening front and dryline around 21Z, with highs in the low 90s and dewpoints in the mid to upper 60s. Initially supercellular storms are possible. Gusts of 65 to 75 mph and large hail are the main hazards, with a tornado or two possible near the front by early evening. The threat should become more isolated overnight, with possible upscale growth into KS/MO and western/southern IL. More isolated severe storms are possible from southwest Texas into the mid Mississippi Valley and parts of New York, where curved low-level hodographs support localized wind damage and a brief tornado. Modest buoyancy limits coverage there.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No SPC Mesoscale Discussions have been issued in the past 6 hours. No organized convective threat is currently under active monitoring by the Storm Prediction Center. No specific systems, locations, or risk categories are being highlighted in this product at this time.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
As of 800 AM EDT Tuesday, October 13, 2026, the Atlantic is quiet. A low-pressure trough several hundred miles west-northwest of the Cabo Verde Islands is producing disorganized showers and storms, but further development is no longer expected. It is moving slowly north to north-northwest within strong upper-level winds. Formation chances are near 0 percent through both 48 hours and 7 days.

As of 500 AM PDT Tuesday, October 13, 2026, the eastern and central North Pacific has two systems of concern. Hurricane Simon is under active advisories, centered about 100 miles west of Cabo Corrientes, Mexico.

Separately, EP93, a low pressure area a few hundred miles south of southern Mexico, is becoming better organized, and satellite-derived winds show a better-defined circulation. Advisories on a tropical depression or tropical storm are likely later today. The system is forecast to move west-northwest near 10 mph. Formation chances are near 100 percent through both 48 hours and 7 days. Interests in southwestern Mexico should monitor its progress, and Gale Warnings are available in the High Seas Forecasts.

sources.title: NHC Active Storm Advisories
sources.summary:
Hurricane Simon, as of 12:00 UTC on 13 October 2026 (5:00 AM MST advisory): maximum sustained winds 90 mph (80 kt, 150 km/h), minimum central pressure 977 mb. The center was about 95 miles west of Cabo Corrientes, Mexico, and 200 miles south-southwest of Mazatlan, moving west-northwest at 3 mph. Simon is a very small hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend about 10 miles from the center and tropical-storm-force winds about 45 miles.

Watches and warnings: a Hurricane Warning is in effect for Las Islas Marias. A Hurricane Watch covers north of Escuinapa to Bahia Tempehuaya, and a Tropical Storm Watch covers Cabo Corrientes to Escuinapa.

Forecast: Simon is expected to move slowly and meander in weak steering currents, with little net motion through about 60 hours. A general northward turn is expected around 96 to 120 hours. Track confidence is very low, and models disagree. Intensity is forecast at 75 kt through 48 hours, weakening to 65 kt by 72 hours and 55 kt by 96 hours. The system is forecast to become post-tropical or inland by 120 hours. Warm waters favor the storm early, but upwelling from slow motion, dry air from land, and increasing shear limit strengthening, and the NHC forecast leans toward the higher end of guidance.

Hazards: Hurricane conditions, especially in gusts, are likely on Las Islas Marias later today or the next day. Tropical-storm conditions are possible in the tropical storm watch area today or Wednesday, and hurricane conditions are possible in the hurricane watch area Thursday. Rainfall of 5 to 10 inches is expected across coastal west-central Mexico, with isolated totals near 15 inches in Sinaloa by Thursday, raising flood and mudslide risk. A dangerous storm surge is possible near Las Islas Marias. Swells will cause life-threatening surf and rip currents along southwestern and west-central Mexican coasts.

Watches and warnings may change today. The next complete advisory is due at 8:00 AM MST.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows El Niño conditions. The latest value, for the JAS 2026 season, is +2.16 degrees C, in the strong El Niño range. The index has risen every season, from -0.39 in DJF 2026 (a cool-phase reading) through +0.46 in MAM, with the first El Niño-threshold value (+0.95) in AMJ. The rise is steepening: the seasonal gain was about 0.35 from MJJ to JJA and 0.36 from JJA to JAS. The sea-surface-temperature total has also risen, from 26.15 to 29.12. The table gives no as-of date and includes no seasons after JAS 2026, so it does not show whether the warming is still accelerating.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary:
Teleconnection indices as of 2026-09-30 (STALE: CPC has not updated these for 13 days, so they do not reflect current conditions).

PNA: +0.12, near neutral and rising. It moved from about -2.0 mid-window to slightly positive, which would favor western North American ridging if it held.

AO: -0.26, near neutral and falling. It dropped from +2.93 at the start of the window, so the strongly positive phase has faded and the index is drifting toward negative, which would favor high-latitude blocking.

NAO: -0.78, falling and the lowest value in the window. This drift negative could make an eastern cutoff less likely to escape.

These are summer values, where extratropical teleconnections are weaker and less reliable. Treat them as directional support only, not as standalone evidence.
